blocks.text: In mathematics, the concepts of limits and continuity are foundational in understanding the behavior of functions and sequences, especially when applied to real-world scenarios. This chapter will introduce and explore how to demonstrate and find the limit of a sequence and a function, understand continuous and discontinuous functions, and apply these concepts in various contexts such as economics, finance, and natural sciences.

This unit will provide you with the tools to understand and apply the fundamental concepts of limits and continuity, both theoretically and practically. By the end, you will be able to demonstrate the limit of a function, test for continuity and discontinuity, and apply these ideas to a wide range of real-world problems across various fields, including finance, economics, and science.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What is a limit, in one sentence? The limit of a function at a point is the value that the function's outputs get closer and closer to when the input gets closer and closer to that point.
A simple picture: walk towards a wall, each step half of the remaining distance. You get as close to the wall as you like, and the wall is where you are heading, even though no single step ends exactly on it. The wall is the limit of your position.
Continuity asks a second question: does the function actually reach that value at the point, with no gap or jump in its graph? You will meet this in 12.3.

blocks.text: The concept of limit of a function is the basis on which the structure of calculus rests. Before the definition of the limit of a function, it is necessary to have a clear understanding of the following phrases.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Calculus (the mathematics of change: speed, slope of a curve, area under a curve) is built on limits. For example, the speed of a car at one instant cannot be found as distance divided by time over zero seconds; it is found as a limit of average speeds over shorter and shorter times.
The phrases the book means are the three that follow on the next pages:
12.1.1 "\(x\) approaches zero" (\(x \to 0\))
12.1.2 "\(x\) approaches infinity" (\(x \to \infty\))
12.1.3 "\(x\) approaches \(a\)" (\(x \to a\))
The arrow \(\to\) is read "approaches" or "tends to". It describes a movement of values, never a single value.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The limit of a function is the value its outputs approach as the input approaches a given point.
2. Limits are the foundation of calculus.
3. The symbol \(\to\) means "approaches" (gets closer and closer to); it is not an equals sign.
4. Unit 12 goes from the idea of a limit (12.1), to working out limits (12.2), to continuity (12.3), to applications (12.4).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(x \to 0\) as "\(x = 0\)". The arrow describes \(x\) coming closer and closer to \(0\), not \(x\) being \(0\) (see the "Point to remember" box in 12.1.3).
2. Thinking a limit is always the value of the function at the point. Often it is, but in 12.2 you will meet many functions whose limit exists at a point where the function itself has no value.
